metadata.title: The Experience of Middle-Income Countries Participating in PISA 2000-2015 (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report synthesises evidence from PISA 2000–2015 and includes descriptive and multilevel analyses based on PISA 2012 mathematics for 18 middle-income countries. For the multilevel analyses described in the report, the authors state that both school and student weights are applied following standard OECD procedures, but the specific weight variable names are not provided in the excerpt. The report also discusses PISA’s complex sampling and the need for comparable implementation across countries, implying that analyses should respect the survey design when estimating standard errors and variance components. Because this is a report-level synthesis rather than a single ML study, the document does not provide a unified, reproducible weighting variable name for all chapters; analysts should follow the OECD PISA technical documentation for the relevant cycle and dataset extract.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The excerpted report text does not provide a single, explicit plausible-values (PV) handling strategy for the full set of analyses across chapters, and it is not a focused empirical ML paper with a clearly defined PV-based dependent variable. While PISA achievement in the multilevel section is described as using all five plausible values, the report does not consistently document PV combining rules and missing-data handling across the entire publication in the provided text. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling are treated as not fully specified at the report level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report’s multilevel analyses focus on PISA 2012 mathematics for 18 middle-income countries: Argentina, Bulgaria, Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Indonesia, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Montenegro, Malaysia, Peru, Romania, Serbia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, and Viet Nam. The excerpt indicates that Albania and Hungary are excluded due to missing student socio-economic status information and income classification, and that China’s PISA 2012 data are excluded except for Shanghai/Hong Kong/Macao which are treated as high-income economies. The multilevel models are specified as two-level student-within-school regressions and use OECD standard procedures, including applying school and student weights; the excerpt does not provide additional task-level or item-level filtering beyond the PISA 2012 mathematics focus.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesises the experiences of middle-income countries participating in PISA from 2000 to 2015, addressing participation deterrents (costs, capacity, context), capacity-building outcomes, policy dialogue, and what PISA data reveal about quality and equity. It includes descriptive comparisons of mathematics performance and proficiency distributions in PISA 2012 across 18 middle-income countries, and it reports multilevel analyses of mathematics performance using PISA 2012 data. In the multilevel section, the outcome is PISA 2012 mathematics performance and the models are two-level student-within-school regressions estimated with maximum likelihood, applying both school and student weights following OECD procedures. The report also documents equity patterns (socioeconomic gradients, language-of-assessment effects, rural–urban gaps) and school stratification (academic and social segregation), and it uses decomposition methods (Oaxaca–Blinder) to explain private/public and vocational/general gaps. Methodologically, the excerpt does not provide a complete, unified PV combining rule and missing-data strategy across all chapters, so cross-chapter comparability of technical choices should be treated cautiously.
